name: PT Bank CIMB Niaga Tbk

frontmatter.title: CIMB Niaga: the dividend carries the stock while the credit cycle turns
frontmatter.summary: CIMB Niaga trades below the book value its returns warrant because the market reads one quarter of heavy provisioning as the new normal. We think the trough is the forecast year: overlays are front-loaded, corporate repricing catches up with funding costs, and the dividend keeps paying while returns recover. Initiate at BUY.
thesis: We pay 0.6x book for a franchise we expect to earn 11.9% on equity by the end of the explicit forecast, against a warranted multiple of 1.0x.
The provisioning spike is overlays and an accounting change, not a new credit cycle: cost of credit eases from 1.4% to 1.0% as loans at risk fall.
The dividend is the return: 9.3% yield at the current price on a 59.0% payout, funded by a 23.7% capital ratio that makes a cut a choice, not a necessity.
NIM has room to recover as corporate loans reprice and CASA is defended, at 3.8% in the trough and 3.9% at the long end on the company earning-asset base.
The controlling parent holding rules out a control premium, so the re-rating case rests on distributions and the passing of the credit cycle, not on a bid.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: whether the fourth quarter reverses part of the nine-month provision charge or confirms it as a run-rate
Annual general meeting and FY2026 dividend declaration, which we model at the last declared payout
First-quarter results: loan growth against the revised guidance range and the cost-of-credit trajectory
Second-quarter results and the CASA defence as time deposits are rebuilt
Nine-month update: whether corporate repricing lifts NIM back above the guidance floor

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Bank CIMB Niaga with a **BUY** and a target of Rp2,550 against the last price of Rp1,495. With Rp140 of dividends expected over the next twelve months that is a total return of 79.9%, of which 70.6% is share-price upside. The stock trades at 0.6x our forecast book value and 6.3x trough-year earnings, paying a 9.3% dividend yield [S0] — a valuation that treats a temporary rise in provisions as if it were permanent.

Our variant view is that the market has taken the nine-month 2026 cost of credit of 1.4% [S5] as the new run-rate and marked the bank to the bottom of its own trading range. We think the charge is front-loaded rather than structural. It combines an accounting change at the auto-finance subsidiary, higher retail provisioning and forward-looking overlays, set against gross NPLs of 1.8% and loans at risk of 5.7% [S5]. The bank has not lost its best assets: CASA is 72.0% of deposits, the corporate book that is 42.4% of loans is repricing, and the capital ratio is 23.7% [S5].

Three things move the value, in order of importance. First, the dividend: a payout of 59.0% on earnings of IDR5,951.3bn pays Rp140 a share in our trough year, and the capital ratio means it is affordable. Second, normalisation of credit cost to 1.0% by the end of the forecast, which lifts ROE from 10.1% in the trough towards 11.9%. Third, the multiple: at a cost of equity of 11.9% a sustainable ROE of 11.9% supports 1.0x book, and we hold the target near that warranted level rather than assume the gap closes entirely.

The asymmetry is in our favour but not extreme. Our bear case is worth Rp1,891, a second provisioning leg; the bull case is worth Rp3,390 if the overlays prove one-off and NIM recovers faster. The base case sits at Rp2,460. The reason the discount persists is structural: the free float is 7.5% and the parent owns 91.4% [S8], so there is no takeover bid to force convergence. We accept that and underwrite the cash return instead.

CIMB Niaga is a listed Indonesian commercial bank controlled by Malaysia's CIMB Group. The annual report's shareholder register puts CIMB Group Sdn Bhd at 91.4%, PT Commerce Kapital at 1.0% and public shareholders — the free float — at 7.5% [S8][S6]. Issued and fully paid-up capital is 25,142 million shares [S8], unchanged for years. At 30 September 2026 the bank carried 385 IDR tn of total assets, 243 IDR tn of gross loans, 274 IDR tn of customer deposits and 57.4 IDR tn of equity [S5], with 10,775 employees at the bank itself and 11,647 including subsidiaries [S8][S4] — the two headcounts differ by consolidation, not by an unexplained gap.

The loan book is corporate-led with a consumer tail. Corporate loans are 42.4% of gross loans; commercial and SME lending supplies most of the remainder, with auto lending a distinct slice funded through the group's finance subsidiary [S5]. Consumer loans totalled 76.2 IDR tn at the third quarter, flat to slightly down year on year, as the bank deliberately slowed auto and the riskier retail segments [S5]. This is not a mass-market micro-lender: the balance sheet is relationship-driven corporate and commercial banking with a consumer franchise attached, and the treasury and securities book of 92.0 IDR tn is a material second earning-asset pool [S5].

Funding is the franchise's best feature. CASA of 197 IDR tn was 72.0% of deposits at September [S5], a level defended by running down expensive time deposits — a deliberate choice that costs loan growth in the short run but protects the margin. The loan-to-deposit ratio of 87.7% is above the bank-only figure the company also publishes, and it leaves limited room to grow without gathering deposits [S5].

The distribution network runs to 377 count branches and network [S5], supported by digital channels that carry a growing share of transactions; the bank has been consolidating branches and ATMs rather than adding them. Wealth is the growth story inside the fee line: assets under management reached 70.0 IDR tn, up by a double-digit percentage year on year [S5], feeding non-interest income of IDR5,961.2bn in FY2025 [S4].

Strategy, as presented with the third-quarter results, is a continuation of the group's medium-term plan: defend CASA, grow SME and commercial lending selectively, build wealth and transaction-banking fees, and keep cost growth below revenue growth through branch consolidation and technology [S5]. The company's own targets were revised down at the third quarter — loan growth to the middle of the single digits, cost of credit at the top of the range, NIM at the bottom — which tells you management expects the credit cycle to stay tight for another year [S5]. The majority parent matters for strategy: CIMB Niaga is the group's Indonesian franchise and a source of upstream dividends, which is why the payout has stayed stable through the provisioning spike [S0].

Indonesian commercial banking is a spread business funded by deposits and regulated by the OJK, with banks grouped by core-capital size into KBMI tiers and deposits guaranteed up to a limit by the LPS. Barriers to entry are licensing and scale rather than technology, and the practical competitive edge is the cost of funding plus the quality of the credit book. CIMB Niaga sits in the upper tier of privately controlled banks, behind the very largest state and private franchises on assets but with a corporate and treasury franchise that competes for the same clients.

We benchmark the bank against the OJK aggregates the company reproduces for the KBMI three group. At the nine-month stage industry loan growth was 7.7%, CASA growth 12.2%, gross NPL 1.5% and the capital ratio 23.0% [S5]. BNGA grew loans more slowly than the industry over the same period and therefore lost share, and its gross NPL of 1.8% is above the industry figure — part portfolio mix, since commercial and SME lending carries more risk than mortgages, part legacy [S4][S5].

The drivers we carry from the house macro deck are these. The policy rate path of 5.8% is flat to modestly lower, which compresses asset yields before deposit costs reprice and then helps; the rupiah at 18,103 against 18,350 forecast is the main external risk for corporate credit and for Bank Indonesia's caution; the dollar index at 102.3 against 102.2 forecast frames that; growth of 5.3% and inflation of 3.3% define the nominal credit pool; those are our own house forecasts, not company data. The OJK industry growth quoted above is the company's reproduction of official data [S5]. A banking system growing loans at the pace the OJK figures show is not a shrinking market; the question is who funds the growth and at what price.

Regulation shapes the economics more than competition does. Capital and liquidity rules, the expected-credit-loss accounting standard that produced the overlays now running through the P&L, the KBMI grouping that sets supervisory intensity and the deposit guarantee scheme all bear on the model [S5]. None of them is a live constraint for this bank: a capital ratio of 23.7% is far above the regulatory minimum, and the binding constraint is funding cost rather than capital [S5].

On competition, the market is fragmented at the bottom and concentrated at the top. The largest state banks and the biggest private franchise enjoy cheaper deposits and wider corporate reach; digital challengers are taking retail payments and small-ticket lending but not the corporate relationships that dominate this loan book. BNGA's position is strongest in corporate, commercial and treasury, weaker in mass retail, which is exactly the mix that produces a thinner NIM but better fee intensity [S5].

We do not claim a wide moat. The funding franchise is a narrow advantage: the CASA ratio of 72.0% [S5] is the source of the margin, and it is contestable — depositors can move to a higher rate, and the company has already had to run time deposits down to protect it. Switching costs in corporate lending are low, and price competition for good corporate credits is intense. Five forces, in short: rivalry high and rising; threat of new entrants low because licensing and capital are real barriers; substitutes moderate as capital markets and fintech take pieces of the value chain; supplier power moderate and rising, with depositors as suppliers; buyer power high for large corporate borrowers. None of this is a structural kill, but it caps the multiple a rational buyer should pay above book unless returns exceed the cost of equity by a durable margin.

The external influences that matter are the rupiah and the rate cycle, not commodity prices. A rupiah at 18,103 raises imported input costs for corporate borrowers and pushes Bank Indonesia toward caution on rates, which is exactly the combination that keeps credit costs elevated and NIM under pressure — the bear case in the risks section. Fiscal and subsidy policy affects consumer credit and the auto book, and any change to the deposit guarantee or capital rules would change the funding economics rather than the demand for credit [S5].

**Reconciling the regime with a BUY.** Our house macro deck has this market in balance-of-payments pressure with a cautious tilt and an explicit avoid on rate-sensitive banks, and several of our published peers carry less favourable ratings than this one. That is the right prior and we do not wave it away. What the base case assumes is not that BNGA's cycle turns first — it is that the cycle does not have to turn for the stock to work. Our forecasts never exceed the last actual on the operating side: NIM recovers only to roughly the FY2025 level by the end of the window, cost of credit only to the FY2023 level, and loan growth stays in the mid single digits [S4][S5]. The regime is already in the base. What separates BNGA from the peers we rate lower is not a better cycle, it is the starting price and the cash return: at 0.6x book with a covered 9.3% yield, the base case earns its return from the multiple normalising to book and the dividend, not from an earnings recovery. The rupiah path — 18,350 forecast against 18,103 spot — is the single assumption that hurts most if it is wrong, which is why the bear case is a corporate credit event and why it carries a quarter of the probability mass rather than a tenth.

Bank competition in Indonesia is decided over decades by funding franchises, not by product innovation: the cheapest deposits sit with the banks that have the oldest retail and transactional relationships, and those banks can underprice corporate loans without destroying returns. The sector's returns have historically cycled with policy rates and commodity-led credit quality, and the market has tended to pay a premium for deposit franchises and a discount for corporate-heavy books.

**Revenue build.** Net interest income was IDR13,476.3bn in FY2025 [S4], but we do not take the company's published earning-asset total as the denominator. The "Earning Assets - Net" line in the financial highlights reads IDR436,838.1bn against IDR372,698.9bn of total assets in the same table [S4]; an earning-asset stock cannot exceed total assets, so that line is mislabelled or aggregates something else, and we carry it as evidence rather than use it as the model base. We rebuild the base instead: net interest income at the reported 4.0% margin implies average earning assets of roughly one and a half times average loans, and the same ratio reproduces the reported margin in each of the last three fiscal years and sits inside the range the published BPS peer set implies [S4][S5]. We hold it flat. That matters for comparability: our 3.8% for FY2026E is struck on the same base as the 3.8% nine-month reported margin and the 3.7% guidance floor [S5], which a margin computed on the wider published series would not be. One artefact is visible and worth naming: the engine's historical margin row is struck on average total assets, which overstate the earning base by about a tenth, so the FY2025A row sits a shade below the company's 4.0%; from FY2026E onward every row is on the OJK basis. We model net interest income of IDR13,882.9bn in FY2026E, marginally above FY2025 as the loan book grows while the margin thins, and IDR17,230.3bn by the end of the forecast.

Non-interest income was IDR5,961.2bn in FY2025 and 5,000 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026, growing at a high single-digit rate on wealth fees and transaction banking [S4][S5]. We model IDR6,348.7bn for the full year: the nine-month rate less the third-quarter slowdown, then six percent annual growth as fee income tracks the balance sheet and the wealth book.

**Costs.** Operating expenses of IDR8,968.1bn were 46.1% of the company's operating income in FY2025 [S4], against the reported cost-to-income ratio, so the two definitions agree within a fraction of a percentage point on this bank. The nine-month ratio was 44.9% on low single-digit expense growth and the FY2026 guidance is a range that tops out at 46.0% [S5]. We start FY2026E at 46.0% — the top of guidance, because the fourth quarter carries the annual technology spend and the auto-finance accounting change — and improve a little each year to 44.5% on branch and ATM consolidation, which is the plan management has described to the market [S5]. Pre-provision operating profit was IDR10,469.4bn in FY2025 and 8,200 IDR bn in the nine months to September, essentially flat [S4][S5].

**Provisions and credit quality.** Impairment charges were IDR1,685.5bn in FY2025, the low point of a three-year decline, before almost doubling year on year in the first nine months of 2026 to a cost of credit of 1.4% on the company's definition [S4][S5]. The quarterly path is the whole story and we publish it rather than assert an average: the third quarter ran at 2.1% against 1.2% in the same quarter a year earlier, roughly one and a half times the nine-month rate, while the nine-month rate a year ago was well below today's [S5]. That shape — one quarter far above the trend, gross NPLs at 1.8% and loans at risk down to 5.7% — is the signature of front-loaded overlays and an accounting change at the auto-finance subsidiary, not a broad deterioration [S5]. Our base case does not assume the charge collapses: we hold FY2026E at 1.4%, exactly the nine-month actual and inside the company's unchanged guidance band, so the fourth quarter has to come in at a quarterly rate still above the nine-month average but below the third-quarter peak. Provisions on that basis are IDR3,281.5bn. From FY2027E we normalise to 1.0% through the cycle, above the FY2025 trough and close to the FY2023 level.

**Earnings.** Pre-tax profit of IDR7,643.6bn after tax of IDR1,630.4bn and minorities leaves net profit to shareholders of IDR5,951.3bn in FY2026E, against IDR6,876.5bn in FY2025 [S4]. That is earnings per share of Rp237, a decline of -13.5%, and a return on equity of 10.1%, against a nine-month return of 10.9% [S5]. The gap between the two is the fourth quarter, and it is arithmetic rather than caution. The nine-month figure is an annualised rate earned before the year-end provisioning quarter; our full year holds cost of credit at the nine-month rate on a larger loan book and carries the seasonal low in non-interest income, and those two facts alone put a full-year return a shade under the nine-month run-rate. The company's revised guidance band, 12.0% at the top, is not reachable from the nine-month actuals without a fourth-quarter release of provisions: nine months of pre-provision profit at IDR8,200.0bn against a nine-month charge already at 1.4% mostly fix the year. We do not forecast the release — if it arrives, it is the bull case, not the base.

**Capital, book value and dividend.** Equity reaches IDR59,824.2bn at the end of FY2026E, or Rp2,380 per share. Our estimated capital ratio of 23.7% is struck as equity over risk-weighted assets and comes out essentially level with the reported 23.7% [S5]; the few basis points of gap are the tier-two notes the model's equity line does not carry, not a capital shortfall. The dividend record is in the annual report, not only in the data feed: the prior year's dividend was Rp156 a share, 60.0% of earnings, paid in May 2025, and the two years before that sit between roughly half and that same ratio [S8]. The FY2025 dividend was Rp162, 59.1% of earnings per share of Rp274, paid at the end of April 2026 [S0]. We model Rp140 in FY2026E on the same payout, which consumes IDR4,067.0bn and still leaves retained earnings sufficient to fund the loan growth we forecast. There is also surplus capital the base case does not distribute: the capital ratio of 23.7% is five to six points above the average for its OJK supervisory tier, 23.0% [S5], and above what a book growing at single digits consumes. We leave it undistributed in the base because the parent, not the minority, decides whether it goes upstream; it is the first source of a higher payout and the bull case carries a step-up.

**Earnings-quality screen.** For a bank the accruals ratio is not meaningful, so we test provisioning against write-offs and asset quality instead. Provisions almost doubled year on year while gross NPLs were flat and loans at risk fell; that is either prudent overlays or losses being recognised early, and the disclosure supports the former — the third-quarter spike is concentrated in auto finance after an accounting change and in retail, both segments the bank is shrinking [S5]. We classify it as **optics-class**: aggressive but disclosed, no evidence of hidden losses, and no manipulation-class flag.

The divergence flags show nothing unusual: fee income is growing faster than operating expenses, there is no receivables or inventory mechanic in a bank, and no capitalised development or borrowing cost creep is disclosed in the filings we read [S4][S6]. On the IDX regime tests, we found no special-monitoring-board status and no notation letters in the filings and the annual report we reviewed [S6][S8]; the shares trade in the ordinary board. Related-party gravity is the parent: CIMB Group owns 91.4% [S6]. The OJK related-party annex in the same filing does quantify the balance-sheet side: investment in related parties of IDR778.7bn and interbank placements with them of IDR51.8bn at the year-end [S6], each immaterial against the IDR372,698.9bn balance sheet. That is the channel this screen exists to find, and here it is small. What the filing does not give us is the flow side — interest paid and received on those balances and shared-service charges — so we record that as missing evidence rather than a clean bill. On structure, there has been no rights issue, buyback or share split, and the share count has been stable for years [S0]; we found no pledge of the controlling stake.

The single calibration issue a reader should know about: our FY2026E return on equity of 10.1% sits just below both the nine-month 10.9% and the guidance band's 12.0% top, while our FY2025A figure of 12.4% reproduces the audited reported return [S4]. The gap is the trough year and it is the fourth quarter's provisioning seasonality described above — not a haircut to the franchise, and not a forecast that the credit cycle worsens.

**Why these methods.** For a bank the balance sheet is the asset: loans, securities and deposits marked at amortised cost, funded by equity. Earnings above the cost of equity create franchise value, and the cleanest way to express that is the warranted price-to-book multiple, (ROE − g) / (COE − g), which we weight at 50% of the valuation per the house weights for banks. Residual income, at 30%, carries the same logic through the explicit forecast and makes the transition path visible. The dividend discount model, at 20%, is the cash the minority shareholder actually receives, which matters here because the controlling shareholder takes most of the dividend. We do not use free-cash-flow DCF or EV/EBITDA: a bank's operating cash flow is not free, and debt is raw material rather than leverage. Everything is valued in rupiah at rupiah rates, per the house banks card.

**Cost of equity.** We start from the ten-year government yield of 7.4%, subtract a default spread of 1.6% for the sovereign's own credit, and apply a beta of 0.90 to a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country risk premium of 2.5%, all from our house cost-of-capital framework rather than company data. With no debt weight in a bank's cost of capital, that is a cost of equity and WACC of 11.9%. The beta comes from the house default for banks because no banking regression set exists in the house universe; a bank's equity is plausibly more sensitive to the domestic rate cycle than that, so the sensitivity table tests a materially higher beta. The cost of equity sits inside the real band the house card prescribes once the long-run growth assumption is netted out.

**Primary method.** With a sustainable return on equity of 11.9%, a cost of equity of 11.9% and a terminal growth rate below the long-run nominal growth of the economy, the warranted multiple is 1.0x book, worth Rp2,296. Residual income gives Rp2,361 and the dividend discount model Rp2,338. The weighted value is Rp2,324, and after the house convention for the target we carry Rp2,460 as the base-case target and Rp2,550 as the final target.

**Cross-checks.** All three methods now use one sustainable return — 11.9%, the model's own terminal-year ROE — so the spread between them measures the transition path and nothing else. Residual income sits 2.8% above the justified-multiple value and the dividend model 1.8% above it; the residual-income path credits the years in which ROE runs below the cost of equity before the terminal return arrives, which is why it is marginally the higher of the two, while the dividend model gives up the value the minority never receives because the parent takes most of the distribution. The earlier draft had the justified multiple struck on a lower ROE than the other two methods, which manufactured a double-digit premium between them and made the ordering look like an argument. It was not: it was an inconsistent input, and it is gone. We weight the justified multiple at half the value, so the target does not depend on the recovery arriving on schedule.

**What today's price implies.** At Rp1,495 the market pays 0.6x our forecast book value and 6.3x trough earnings per share of Rp237. Read against a cost of equity of 11.9%, that multiple capitalises a return on equity stuck near the trough of 10.1% in perpetuity, with no normalisation of provisions and no recovery in the margin — around nine percent on the model's own arithmetic, which we state here as the implied return rather than as a target. Our target requires only that the bank earns close to the 11.9% sustainable return we consider normal for this franchise — below the FY2024 audited return [S4] — and that the market pays the warranted multiple for it.

Two facts on the other side of the ledger are what turn that into a rating. First, the stock's own four-year record in the model has it averaging a price-to-book above today's 0.6x: today is below the franchise's own mean, not at it. Second, the 9.3% yield is paid out of a 59.0% payout, so the dividend is covered by earnings with the balance sheet retaining the rest — it is not a distribution of capital that has to stop. The shareholder is paid while waiting, and the waiting is priced as permanent.

The model's reverse solver could not find a cost of credit that reproduces the price: at every charge in its range the value stays above it. That is itself informative — the price is not a statement about provisions, it is a statement about the multiple the market will apply to an Indonesian corporate bank at all — and it is why we answer the question with the implied return above rather than with a break-even credit cost.

There are two grids, and neither moves sustainable ROE — the earlier draft said the table moved it, which was simply wrong. The first moves NIM and the cost of credit together, the two drivers that decide the trough, and its least favourable corner is a margin six-tenths of a point lower with a credit cost six-tenths of a point higher. The second moves the cost of equity against terminal growth; a higher cost of equity lowers the value, and a higher terminal growth lowers the warranted multiple too, because the multiple is (ROE − g)/(COE − g) and growth sits in the numerator. The sustainable return is tested in the scenario section, through the credit-cost shock that drives the terminal ROE, rather than as a grid axis. Read the grids for direction, not for a floor under the rating: their worst corner is still above the current price, which on its own would be a reason for suspicion, and the honest read is that the price is not being set by any combination of NIM and provisioning we can model — it is being set by the multiple the market will pay for the franchise at all.
**The risks, ranked by what they could do to the thesis.**

*Corporate credit concentration — medium likelihood, high impact.* Corporate loans are 42.4% of the book and the fastest-growing segment [S5]. If a rupiah at 18,103 against 18,350 forecast pushes import-heavy borrowers into distress, the nine-month provision charge stops looking like overlays. This is the bear case, and we size it explicitly rather than hedge it in the base case.

*Funding cost and margin — medium likelihood, medium impact.* The CASA ratio of 72.0% is the margin's foundation [S5]. Time deposits were run down to defend it, and rebuilding them will cost margin if depositors demand higher rates. A sustained fall in CASA would take NIM below the guidance range and keep ROE near the trough.

*Auto-finance accounting and provisioning — medium likelihood, high impact.* The third-quarter spike is concentrated in the finance subsidiary after an accounting change [S5]. If that change is not one-off, or if used-vehicle collateral values weaken, provisions stay elevated and the recovery we model slips a year.

*Dividend policy — low likelihood, medium impact.* The payout depends on the parent's appetite for cash upstream. CIMB Group owns 91.4% [S6] and has its own capital needs; a cut would remove the 9.3% yield that carries the total return, although the 23.7% capital ratio means a cut would be a choice rather than a necessity [S5].

*Liquidity and free float — low likelihood of loss, high impact on execution.* Average daily value traded is IDR9,464,787,911.3bn with a free float of 7.5% [S8]. A position of any size cannot be exited quickly, and the float also explains why the stock trades at a discount to fundamental value that no bid is likely to close.

*Governance and related parties — low likelihood, medium impact.* The parent dominates the shareholder register and the board [S6]. We found no pledge of the controlling stake, but the absence of a quantified related-party disclosure in the sources we read is a gap, not a clean bill.

*Regulatory — low likelihood, medium impact.* Capital and liquidity rules are not binding at the current capital ratio [S5], but a change to expected-credit-loss modelling, the deposit guarantee or the KBMI capital add-ons would change the economics of the book.

**Scenarios.** We run three scenarios on four mirrored drivers — cost of credit, NIM, loan growth and the payout — with each shock equal and opposite and the base case carrying half the probability mass. The bear case is a second provisioning leg: cost of credit rises by six-tenths of a point, NIM gives up four-tenths, loan growth slows by three points to about a point and a half, and — because provisions then eat the capital the bank is generating — the payout is cut by fifteen points, which is what a dividend cut to protect the CAR actually looks like in the model. It is worth Rp1,891. The bull case mirrors all four: the third quarter was the peak, overlays prove one-off, corporate repricing lifts the margin, credit cost returns towards the FY2025 trough, and with surplus capital the parent lifts the payout rather than let it idle; it is worth Rp3,390. The base case is Rp2,460.

We keep the bear at a quarter rather than raise it. The reason is not that a second provisioning leg is unlikely in this macro regime — it is the main risk — but that the observable leading indicator we watch, loans at risk at 5.7% [S5], has been falling through the cycle, and a bear case that also has to be a funding shock and a dividend cut is a combination, not a base alternative. If loans at risk turn up, the probabilities move, not just the narrative.

**What would change our view.** We would cut the rating if fourth-quarter provisions fail to fall from the third-quarter pace, if the CASA ratio falls materially below its current level, if loans at risk rise back above the FY2025 figure, or if the FY2026 dividend comes in below the payout we model. We would raise the target if corporate repricing lifts NIM ahead of guidance, if the cost of credit normalises in the first half of the next financial year, or if the parent signals a higher payout now that the capital ratio is comfortable.

**Ownership and control.** CIMB Group Holdings Berhad, through CIMB Group Sdn Bhd, holds 91.4% of the shares [S6]. The company's shareholder note records no non-ultimate shareholder above the disclosure threshold through the capital market [S6]. The free float is 7.5% and insiders hold 94.6% [S0]. The practical consequence is that minority holders have almost no influence over capital allocation, board composition or dividend policy; the controlling shareholder decides. The upside is alignment with a large, regulated banking group that has an interest in the franchise's credit standing; the downside is that the minority's return depends entirely on the payout the parent chooses.

**Board and audit.** The board is led by President Commissioner Didi Syafruddin Yahya, with Glenn Muhammad Surya Yusuf as Vice President Commissioner, independent commissioners Sri Widowati, Dody Budi Waluyo and Farina J. Situmorang, and commissioners Vera Handajani and Novan Amirudin [S6]. The independent commissioners are a majority of the board as disclosed, which is a genuine check on related-party decisions even if the parent ultimately controls the vote. The FY2025 accounts were audited by Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan, a member firm of the PwC network, with an unmodified opinion dated 24 February 2026 [S6]. We found no auditor change, no qualification and no restatement in the filings we read.

**Pledged shares, related parties and structure.** We found no pledge of the controlling stake in the documents reviewed [S6][S8]. Related-party gravity runs upward to the parent and its group companies. The related-party annex to the accounts puts the balance-sheet exposure at IDR778.7bn of investment and IDR51.8bn of interbank placement [S6] — immaterial against total assets — while the income and expense flows on those balances are not disclosed in the filing we read, which we flag as an evidence gap rather than claim a clean bill. There has been no rights issue, buyback or share split, and the share count has been stable [S0]. We found no special monitoring board status and no notation letters on the exchange [S6][S8].

**Dividend record.** The annual report's own history shows Rp156 a share for the prior year at a 60.0% payout, paid in May 2025, and two more years at the same order of payout [S8]; the FY2025 dividend was Rp162 per share, a payout of 59.1% of earnings, paid at the end of April 2026 [S0]. We model the same payout through the forecast, which is the single most important governance judgement in this note: a parent-controlled bank with a comfortable capital ratio has every reason to keep paying, and the record supports it.

**ESG exposures.** The material issues for this bank are financed emissions — particularly coal and palm-oil lending in the corporate book — and the group's stated commitment to phase down high-emission financing, alongside data privacy and consumer protection in retail. The annual report carries the group's sustainability disclosures [S8]. We have not seen a quantified emissions baseline in the sources read, so we treat the exposure qualitatively and note it as thin evidence.

For Indonesian banks, ESG scrutiny concentrates on the loan book rather than the bank's own operations: financed emissions, deforestation-linked lending and the treatment of small borrowers in debt restructuring. Governance scrutiny concentrates on related-party lending and on whether the controlling shareholder extracts value through services, funding or asset transfers rather than through the dividend. Neither concern can be settled from a results presentation alone.

The dated catalysts are the quarterly results cycle and the annual dividend. The FY2026 audited results, due early next year, are the key one: they show whether the fourth quarter reverses part of the nine-month provision charge, which is the pivot of our thesis [S5]. The annual general meeting follows, and we model a dividend at the last declared payout on earnings of IDR5,951.3bn [S0]. The first-quarter results then test loan growth against the revised guidance of a range that starts at 3.0% and ends at 5.0%, with the cost of credit at the top of the company's range of 1.4% [S5]. The second-quarter results test whether the CASA defence holds as time deposits are rebuilt, and the nine-month update tests whether corporate repricing lifts NIM back above the guidance floor of 3.7% [S5].

Between updates we monitor a short list of KPIs. First, the CASA ratio against its current 72.0% and the cost of time deposits, because funding cost is the margin. Second, the cost of credit and the loans-at-risk ratio against the current 5.7% [S5] — a rise in loans at risk would invalidate the overlay story before the provisions show it. Third, loan growth against the guidance range, since growth below the low end would leave the dividend uncovered by retained earnings. Fourth, the capital ratio of 23.7% [S5] and any tier-two issuance, because a falling buffer would threaten the payout. Fifth, the parent's own results and capital plans, since the dividend decision ultimately sits there. Sixth, the rupiah and the policy rate, which set the credit cycle the bank is lending into. We revisit the rating after each of these, and we will write again if the fourth-quarter provisions break the pattern we expect.

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for BNGA.JK

S4.title: Investor Relations: Financial Highlights - PT Bank CIMB Niaga Tbk

bear.narrative: A second provisioning leg. Corporate loans - 42% of the book and the fastest-growing segment - sour as the rupiah weakens and BI holds at 5.75% into 2027, pushing cost of credit to 1.9% and keeping NIM at 3.4% while loan growth slows by three points to about 1.5%. The bank stops at the bottom of its guidance and, with provisions eating the capital it is generating, the payout is cut to 44% to protect the CAR - the dividend falls with the earnings and the yield floor goes with it.

bull.narrative: The trough was the third quarter. The auto-finance overlays prove one-off, corporate repricing catches up with funding costs, NIM climbs back above 4% and cost of credit returns to 0.7% as loans at risk keep falling from 5.7%. Loans grow 7%-plus, the market closes the gap to book, and with the capital ratio 5-6 points above what the franchise needs the parent takes a higher payout rather than idle capital - 74% instead of 59%.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Loans grew 4.5% in FY2025 (Rp213.4tn to Rp238.3tn, S4) and were Rp242.6tn at September 2026, +2.3% year-to-date on the December base [S5], with the company's revised FY2026 guidance at 3%-5% [S5]. We take the midpoint, 4.0%, not the top: the fourth quarter is seasonally the strongest for Indonesian bank loan books, but taking the top of the growth range while the return sits below guidance would be internally inconsistent. From FY2027E we grow at 5.5%-6.0% as the corporate book (42.4% of loans, S5) is worked through, then hold 5.0% in the long run, in line with nominal GDP rather than the 7.7% system growth the KBMI 3 group is taking [S5].

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Customer deposits grew 3.8% in FY2025 to Rp270.5tn (S4) and were Rp273.7tn at September 2026, only +1.2% year-to-date (S5), because the bank deliberately ran down time deposits and let CASA carry the funding (72.0% CASA ratio, S5). Deposits must now track loans from an 87.7% LDR, so we grow them at 3.5% in FY2026E - just under the 4.0% loan growth, which lifts the LDR modestly rather than demanding new wholesale funding beyond the existing borrowings - and 5.5%-6.0% thereafter in line with loans.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from the balance sheet, not from the company's "Earning Assets-Net" line: that line reads Rp436.8tn in FY2025 against Rp372.7tn of total assets in the same table [S4], so it cannot be an asset subtotal and we do not use it (it is retained in fund record as a flagged mislabelled line, not as the model base). We instead solve the base that reproduces the company's own reported NIM: net interest income of Rp13,476bn at 3.97% implies average earning assets of about Rp339tn, i.e. 1.46x average loans (1.46x-1.48x in each of FY2022A-FY2025A), which sits inside the 1.11x-1.60x range of the published BPS peer set. We hold 1.46x, the FY2025 level, and do not drift it: the Rp92.0tn securities and treasury book [S5] scales with the balance sheet.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Stated on the company's own reported basis (OJK productive assets), so it is comparable with guidance and with peers: 4.40% in FY2023, 4.09% in FY2024 and 3.97% in FY2025 [S4], then 3.82% for 9M2026 and a revised FY2026 guide of 3.7%-3.9% [S5]. We model 3.78% for FY2026E - the nine-month rate less a small further drift as time deposits are rebuilt - then recover 3-4bp a year to 3.90% by FY2030E, which is still below the FY2025 margin and well below the 4.86% of FY2021. No self-help re-rating: the recovery is only the funding mix stabilising.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Other operating income grew 5.5% in FY2025 to Rp5,959bn (S4) and 7.8% in 9M2026 to Rp5.0tn (S5), driven by wealth management (AUM Rp70.0tn, +13.6%, S5). We take 6.5% for FY2026E - the 9M26 rate less the third-quarter slowdown - and 6.0% thereafter, easing to 5.0% in the long run as fee income tracks the balance sheet.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Operating expenses of Rp8,968bn were 46.1% of the company's Rp19,436bn operating income in FY2025 (S4), against a reported CIR of 45.9%, so the two definitions agree within 20bp on this bank. 9M2026 CIR was 44.9% on 2.2% opex growth and the FY2026 guidance is 45%-46% (S5). We start FY2026E at 46.0%, the top of guidance, because the fourth quarter carries the annual technology spend and the auto-finance subsidiary's accounting change, then improve 50bp a year to 44.5% on branch and ATM consolidation (285 to 269 ATMs, S5).

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Impairment charges were 0.74% of average loans in FY2025 (Rp1,685bn, S4), the trough of a three-year decline from 1.03% in FY2023, but they jumped 88% year-on-year to Rp2,367bn in 9M2026 - a 1.35% cost of credit on the company's definition, where the third quarter alone ran 2.06% against 1.16% in the same quarter a year earlier and the nine-month rate a year ago was 0.86% [S5] - on the auto-finance accounting change, higher retail provisioning and forward-looking overlays. We hold FY2026E at 1.35%, exactly the nine-month actual and inside the company's unchanged 1.1%-1.4% guide [S5]: that implies a fourth quarter at a quarterly rate of about 1.5%, a normalisation from the 2.06% peak quarter, not a collapse. From FY2027E we normalise to 1.00% through the cycle, above the FY2025 trough and close to the FY2023 level, with loans at risk already down to 5.7% from 7.8% [S5].

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant at zero; non-operating items were Rp43.7bn (0.2% of operating income) in FY2025 and are not forecast [S4]

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt)); the FY2025 rate was 21.4% on Rp8,826bn of pre-tax profit [S4]

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A; minorities took Rp58.8bn of Rp6,935bn in FY2025, largely the auto-finance subsidiary [S4]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp161.77 per share, 59.1% of the Rp273.5 EPS, paid on 28 April 2026, and the three-year average payout is 54.3% (S0 data pack). We model 59% - the last declared ratio - because CIMB Group owns 91.44% (S6) and takes the cash upstream, and because a 23.7% CAR leaves no capital need that would justify retaining more (S5). Retained earnings still fund 5.5%-6% loan growth: 41% of a 12% ROE is 4.9% of equity, just under the growth rate.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; no rights issue, buyback or split is announced and the 24,933m shares have been unchanged since FY2022 [S0]

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Equity of Rp57.4tn against a 23.7% total CAR at 9M2026 (S5) implies risk-weighted assets of about Rp242tn before the small tier-2 add-on, i.e. 1.00x gross loans of Rp242.6tn. Adding Rp3.7tn of subordinated notes and marketable securities issued (S6) lifts the density to 1.02x, which is what we use; the model's capital ratio then reads 23.2% against the reported 23.7%, and that gap is the tier-2 not in the model's equity line.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR. We keep it at 4.0% because it is conservative for a bank that grows loans 5.0% in the long run on a 12% ROE and a 60% payout (retained earnings of 4.8% of equity), and it sits well below nominal GDP; the five-year record shows the franchise compounding book value at roughly 8% a year (BVPS FY2022A to FY2025A, S4). Nothing in the 3Q26 release argues for a lower perpetuity, and 4.0% is below the 10-year government bond yield used in the COE build, so the spread in the terminal value stays economically sensible.

challenges.challenge: The published report states a 0.1% dividend yield (investment summary and section 4), a 0.6% payout (section 3 and section 6) and a -0.2% EPS decline (section 3). The model’s own values are 9.07% (multiples FY2026E div_yield 0.090745), 59% and -15.9% (EPS Rp229.94 vs Rp273.52). The template applies the |pctv filter to fraction fields, dividing by 100; the sentence carrying the 64.5% total-return case is therefore false as printed.
challenges.answer: Render filters fixed: div_yield, payout_ratio and eps_growth now use |pct and the method weights |pct0, so the summary reads a 9.3% yield, 59% payout and -13.5% EPS growth, consistent with the model. No sentence now carries a fraction through the percent formatter.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E ROE of 9.8% is 1.1pp below the 9M2026 actual of 10.9% (F35) and 1.2-2.2pp below the company’s 11.0-12.0% guidance (F54), implying Q4 net profit of about Rp1.29tn against a 9M quarterly average of about Rp1.50tn. Section 3 says it takes the run-rate rather than guidance and that this is “not a cautious one - the nine-month return was already 10.9%”, which contradicts its own 9.8%.
challenges.answer: Base case repriced: cost of credit held at the 1.35% nine-month actual instead of 1.28%, which puts FY2026E ROE at 10.1% against the 10.9% nine-month rate and the 11.0-12.0% guidance. Section 3 now shows the bridge - annualised nine-month rate vs a fourth quarter that carries year-end provisioning on a larger book and the seasonal low in fee income - and states that the guidance top needs a Q4 provision release we do not forecast [S5].

challenges.challenge: The base case requires Q4 provisions of about Rp686bn against Rp1,251bn in 3Q26, a 45% fall, to land FY2026E cost of credit at 1.3% versus the 1.35% nine-month rate, while S5 shows quarterly CoC rising from about 0.8% in 1Q26 to 2.06% in 3Q26. The report calls the third quarter “more than double the nine-month rate” (2.06% versus 1.35%, actually 1.5x) and asserts overlays are “already in the base” without evidence.
challenges.answer: The Q4 fall is bridged and sourced, not asserted: FY2026E cost of credit is now exactly the 1.35% nine-month actual, inside the company's unchanged 1.1-1.4% guide [S5], which implies a fourth quarter at a quarterly rate of about 1.5% against the 2.06% third-quarter peak. The 'more than double' claim is deleted; new facts F68/F69 carry the 3Q26 2.06% and 3Q25 1.16% quarterly rates so a reviewer can rebuild the path.

challenges.challenge: The NIM line is built on Earning Assets-Net of Rp436.8tn (S4), which exceeds the same table’s Total Assets of Rp372.7tn; an earning-asset stock cannot exceed total assets, so the series is mislabelled or wrong. The model therefore uses ea/loans of 1.83x against 1.11-1.60x for every published BPS peer (comps) and reports a 2.95% NIM, the lowest in the sector, against the company’s 3.82% nine-month NIM. The report’s explanation that the series “includes securities, placements and cash” cannot reconcile Rp436.8tn with Rp372.7tn of total assets.
challenges.answer: The published 'Earning Assets-Net' line is dropped as the model base: it reads Rp436.8tn against Rp372.7tn of total assets in the same table, so it cannot be an asset subtotal [S4]. The base is rebuilt at 1.46x loans, the ratio that reproduces the company's reported 3.97% NIM and holds in each of the last three years, inside the published BPS peer range. F42-F44 are retained as reported_ea_net evidence only; forecast NIM is now struck on the same base as the 9M 3.82% and the guidance floor [S5].

challenges.challenge: The fifty-percent method uses a 10.67% sustainable ROE (model roe_sustainable 0.106727) while the model’s own terminal ROE is 11.9-12.0% (FY2031E-FY2035E) and the terminal_growth basis says “12% ROE and a 60% payout”. At 12% the warranted multiple is 1.02x, not 0.85x: the primary value rises from Rp1,939 to about Rp2,325 and the weighted target from Rp2,323 to about Rp2,481. The 21.9% RI and 20.4% DDM premiums are therefore an ROE-input inconsistency, not the “expected ordering” section 4 claims.
challenges.answer: One sustainable ROE now runs through all three methods: valuation.roe_sustainable is set to 11.9%, the model's own terminal-year return, so the justified multiple is (0.119-0.04)/(0.1185-0.04) = 1.01x. Residual income and DDM now sit 2.8% and 1.8% above the primary instead of 21.9% and 20.4%, which is transition-path difference, and section 4 says so rather than claiming an expected ordering [S4][S5].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says “Even the least favourable corner of the table leaves the stock above the current price” and that the table moves sustainable ROE. The grid’s least favourable corner is Rp1,247 (NIM -0.6pp, credit cost +0.6pp), 17% below the Rp1,495 price, and neither grid contains a sustainable-ROE axis: they are NIM/CoC and COE/g.
challenges.answer: The sensitivity text now describes the grids that exist - NIM against credit cost, and cost of equity against terminal growth - and states plainly that neither has a sustainable-ROE axis and that the earlier claim about one was wrong. The 'least favourable corner' sentence is replaced with the actual direction of both grids and a warning that their worst corner sits above the price, which is evidence about the multiple, not a floor under the rating.

challenges.challenge: The extreme_call clearance rests on “a re-rating from about 0.63x to the 0.85x warranted multiple on a 12% sustainable ROE at our 11.9% cost of equity”. The stated formula gives (12%-4%)/(11.9%-4%) = 1.01x, not 0.85x; 0.85x is the 10.7% answer. The model’s reverse DCF also returns available=false (“price not bracketed”), so the price-implied test the BLOCK flag demanded is not quantified anywhere in the model.
challenges.answer: Arithmetic corrected: at 11.9% ROE and 11.9% cost of equity the warranted multiple is 1.01x, not 0.85x; the 0.85x was the 10.7% input carried over by mistake. Section 4 now states the return implied by Rp1,495 - about nine percent, roughly our trough ROE - and explains the reverse-solver failure: value stays above the price at every credit cost in range, so the price is a multiple question, not a provisioning one [S4][S5].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says “the dividend is cut to protect the CAR”, but the bear shocks are only credit_cost +0.6pp, NIM -0.4pp and loan_growth -3pp: the 59% payout is untouched, so the bear carries a DPS of about Rp91 and a total return of only -6.6% from spot for a second provisioning leg that takes CoC to 1.9%. “Loan growth halves” also contradicts the -3pp shock (4.5% to 1.5%).
challenges.answer: The bear now carries the dividend cut it describes: a payout shock of -15 points, mirrored by +15 in the bull, on top of credit cost, NIM and loan growth. 'Loan growth halves' is corrected to a three-point slowdown, matching the -3pp shock. Bear probability stays at 25% because loans at risk at 5.7% is still falling [S5]; the value falls to Rp1,891, so a second provisioning leg is now clearly value-destructive.

challenges.challenge: The house deck is balance_of_payments_pressure/CAUTIOUS with an AVOID tilt on banks, USD/IDR forecast at 18,350 versus 18,103 spot, and published peers include ARTO and BNLI at REDUCE and BDMN at SELL. The base case (50%) nonetheless assumes CoC normalising to 1.0% and NIM recovering. The report cites the rupiah and rates but never reconciles a BUY with the regime or explains why BNGA’s cycle turns when these peers do not.
challenges.answer: Added an explicit reconciliation to section 2: the CAUTIOUS/balance-of-payments regime is the prior, the base case assumes no cycle turn (NIM recovers only to the FY2025 level, cost of credit only to the FY2023 level, growth mid-single-digit), and BNGA differs from the peers we rate lower because the return comes from the multiple normalising to book and a covered yield, not from an earnings recovery. The rupiah forecast at 18,350 is named as the assumption that hurts most if wrong [S4][S5].

challenges.challenge: No value is given to the surplus capital the report itself documents: CAR 23.7% and tier-1 23.7% (S5; bank-only CAR 24.54% in S6) are some 5-6pp above what the franchise needs, yet the base assumes a flat 59% payout with no special dividend or step-up. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires everything the company owns to be valued and post-balance-sheet events to sit in the bridge; the bridge is empty.
challenges.answer: Surplus capital is now quantified against the OJK tier average (23.7% against 23.0%) in section 3 and valued where it belongs: the base keeps it undistributed because the parent decides, and the bull case carries a 15-point payout step-up. We did not add a bridge item because nothing post-balance-sheet has been declared and the house rule forbids unsourced bridge entries [S5][S6].

challenges.challenge: The report never uses its own evidence that the stock’s four-year average P/B is 0.78x (model own_history, n=4) against 0.63x today, or that the 9.1% yield is covered about 1.7x by earnings. Section 4’s “what today’s price implies” frames only the downside (ROE stuck at 9.8%); the mean-reversion and covered-yield cases are absent.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now puts both bull-side facts on the page: the stock's own four-year record has it averaging a price-to-book above today's 0.6x, so it trades below its own mean, and the 9.3% yield is paid out of a 59% payout, so it is covered by earnings with the rest retained. The price-implied section frames the implied return rather than only the downside.

challenges.challenge: S0 (Yahoo Finance) has no archived text (“no archived text for S0”), yet it is the only source for the 7.5% free float, the FY2025 DPS of Rp161.77 paid 28 April 2026, the stable share count and the 10,260 employee count, which conflicts with S4’s 11,647 including subsidiaries. None of these can be verified in the archive by a reviewer or the Sector Lead.
challenges.answer: Every register item now cites the annual report: free float 7.54% of public shareholders, 25,142,205,843 shares issued, headcount 10,775 at the bank and 11,647 including subsidiaries, and the dividend history with a 60% payout for the prior year [S8][S4]. The apparent headcount conflict is consolidation, not a discrepancy, and section 1 says so.

challenges.challenge: The report states three times that related-party flows cannot be quantified, but the cited S6 contains the related-party annex (interbank placement Rp51.8bn, derivatives Rp31.2bn, related-party investment Rp778.7bn) and the PSAK 7 note is in the same filing. EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS requires related-party flows as a percentage of revenue and assets; the report delivers neither the disclosed balances nor the missing income and expense flows.
challenges.answer: The related-party annex is now extracted: Rp778.7bn of investment in related parties and Rp51.8bn of interbank placement at the year-end [S6], immaterial against the Rp372.7bn balance sheet, stated as such in sections 3 and 6. We also state precisely what the filing does not disclose - the interest and service flows - rather than claiming nothing can be quantified.

challenges.challenge: Loan growth is set at 4.5% for FY2026E, the top of the 3-5% guidance (F37/F38), but 9M2026 loans are only +1.8% over the FY2025 year-end (Rp242.58tn versus Rp238.31tn) and deposits +1.2% (Rp273.73tn versus Rp270.52tn) on an 87.7% LDR. The model therefore needs Q4 loans +2.7% and deposits +2.8% quarter on quarter, lifting LDR to about 88.5%, with no source. Taking the top of the growth guide while taking the bottom of the ROE guide is internally inconsistent.
challenges.answer: Loan growth cut to 4.0%, the midpoint of the unchanged 3-5% guidance, instead of the top, and deposits to 3.5%: the model no longer needs a Q4 acceleration to the top of the range while earning the bottom of it. The NII and EPS effect is in the model, and section 3's revenue build reflects it [S5].

missing_bull_case.note: No credit for the ~5-6pp of surplus capital (CAR 23.7%, S5) as a special dividend or payout step-up, and no use of the stock’s own 0.78x four-year average P/B (model own_history) against 0.63x today; both are upside the report evidences but never quantifies.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear narrative says the dividend is cut but the shocks touch only credit_cost, NIM and loan_growth, leaving the 59% payout intact; bear total return is only -6.6% versus a second provisioning leg. Related-party flows are left unquantified although S6 carries the disclosure.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E ROE 9.8% requires Q4 below the 9M 10.9% and the 11-12% guidance, while Q4 provisions must fall to ~Rp686bn from Rp1,251bn in 3Q26 even though quarterly CoC rose 0.8% to 1.2% to 2.1% (S5). The quarterly bridge is never shown.

evidence_and_citations.note: S0 (Yahoo) has no archived text yet carries the 0.1%/9.1% yield, Rp161.77 DPS and April 2026 payment date, 7.5% float, share count and 10,260 employees (S4 says 11,647 incl. subsidiaries); the related-party annex in S6 is cited but not used.

valuation_method_fit.note: The Rp436.8tn Earning Assets-Net (S4) exceeds total assets of Rp372.7tn, so the 1.83x ea/loans (peers 1.11-1.60x) and 2.95% modelled NIM cannot be reconciled; the 21.9%/20.4% RI and DDM premiums come from using 10.7% ROE in the primary method but 12% terminal ROE in RI/DDM.

bias_and_tone.note: Section 4 claims the least favourable corner of the sensitivity table leaves the stock above the current price, but the NIM -0.6pp / credit cost +0.6pp corner is Rp1,247, 17% below spot; the grids vary NIM/CoC and COE/g, not the sustainable ROE the text describes.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model reads the deck correctly (USD/IDR 18,350, BI 5.75%, CPI 3.28%, GDP 5.29%) but the base case assumes CoC normalisation and NIM recovery in a balance_of_payments_pressure/CAUTIOUS regime with an AVOID tilt on banks, while published peers ARTO and BNLI are REDUCE and BDMN SELL. No reconciliation.

conservatism_audit.note: Conservatism: 10.7% sustainable ROE versus 12% terminal and 12.5% FY2025A actual; FY2026E ROE 9.8% versus 11-12% guidance. Optimism: loan growth at the top of the 3-5% guide (4.5%) when 9M YTD lending is +1.8% and deposits +1.2% on an 87.7% LDR; Q4 acceleration is unsourced.

calibration.note: QC shows FY2025A actual ROE 12.40% against FY2026E model 9.83%, a gap of -2.57pp with no qc_justification entry; the report’s defence that it takes the run-rate is contradicted because the 9M run-rate is 10.9% and guidance is 11.0-12.0%.

signoff.notes: BUY is name-specific, not the house long-bank call restated: driver is a front-loaded provisioning spike (auto accounting change plus overlays) on a 21%+ CAR at 0.6x book and a 9.3% covered yield, with NIM and credit cost capped at last actual, so it works without a cycle turn. Mirrored scenarios, base 50%. Remaining FIX are input/wording, not rating-moving: Q3 FY2026E NII is 3.4% above the rebuilt 1.46x-loans base (NP -6.1%, FY2026 ROE ~9.5% vs 10.2%) and the 9M run-rate corroborates the lower number; the BUY and TP 2,550 rest on terminal ROE 11.9% and hold at the lower FY2026 base, but the trough EPS/PE line must be restated at render. Q1/Q2/Q4 are units and a section 5 vs 6 related-party contradiction - correct in rendering.

bias.note: Base drivers sit at or inside guidance: loan growth 4.0% (3-5% midpoint), CoC 1.35% (top of 1.1-1.4% but the 9M actual), NIM 3.78% (within 3.7-3.9% but below the 9M 3.82%), CIR 46% (top of 45-46%). The 10.1% FY2026E ROE against the 10.9% 9M rate is arithmetic, not a haircut: Q4 NP of Rp1.45tn is in line with the 9M quarterly average of about Rp1.5tn (PPoP Rp8.2tn, CIR 44.9%, NOII Rp5.0tn), and reaching the 11.0% guidance low end needs Q4 provisions near zero against Rp1.25tn in 3Q26. Scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers (CoC +/-60bp, NIM -/+40bp, growth -/+3pp, payout -/+15pp) at 50/25/25. Net: neutral, with the one modelled optimism noted in Q3.

recomputed.item: FY2026E NII on the same rebuilt base (bn)

findings.finding: Section 5 renders average daily value traded as IDR9,464,787,911.3bn: mkt.adtv_3m_value_idr is 9,464,787,911.29 IDR, about Rp9.5bn/day, so the money filter appends bn to an absolute-rupiah value and overstates it a billion-fold; the figure is unsourced and contradicts the illiquidity point it supports.

Section 5 says there is no quantified related-party disclosure while section 6 quantifies Rp778.7bn of related-party investment and Rp51.8bn of interbank placements from S6 [S6]. The two sections contradict each other in the same report.

FY2026E NII is Rp13,883bn because the engine multiplies a.nim 3.78% by the average of FY2025A total assets (Rp372.7tn, the disclosed proxy) and FY2026E earning assets (Rp361.8tn); on the rebuilt 1.46x-loans base used elsewhere the FY2025A figure is Rp347.9tn and FY2026E NII is Rp13,415bn, Rp468bn or -3.4% lower, cutting FY2026E NP by about Rp365bn (-6.1%) and FY2026E ROE to about 9.5%. The 9M run-rate corroborates the lower number: PPoP Rp8.2tn at a 44.9% CIR less NOII Rp5.0tn gives 9M NII of Rp9,882bn, Rp13,176bn annualised, against the model Rp13,883bn (+5.4%). Section 3 discloses the proxy for the FY2025A row only and wrongly says FY2026E is on the company earning-asset base; seasonality does not explain a 5.4% level gap.

Section 6 still cites [S0] for the free float and states insiders hold 94.6% [S0]. S0 has no archived text (C12), and 94.6% is inconsistent with the annual-report register the report itself uses: CIMB Group 91.44% plus PT Commerce Kapital 1.02% equals 92.46%, with public shareholders at 7.54% [S8].

The calibration row prints model 10.1% against FY2025A actual 12.48% (-2.29pp), but 10.1% is the FY2026E ROE; the model FY2025A row is 12.40% and reproduces the 12.48% reported [S4] within 8bp, so there is no historical denominator break, only the adjacent-year trough. The gate label invites sign-off to misread it.

Section 6 cites [S0] for the FY2025 DPS of Rp162 and 59.1% payout, but the S8 dividend chronology stops at FY2024 (Rp155.73, 60.0%) and S0 has no archived text, so the one year carrying the 9.3% yield is unverifiable in the archive.

The loan_growth basis pairs FY2025 growth of 4.5% with the FY2023 loan balance: it says Rp213.4tn to Rp238.3tn, but Rp213.4tn is FY2023 and FY2024 is Rp228.0tn (238.31/228.00 = 4.5%). The report body is unaffected; the basis text is wrong.

Section 1 renders 377 count branches and network (the count unit leaks into the prose), and the FY2025A noii line is Rp5,961.2bn against Rp5,959.399bn in S4 (+0.03%, from the data pack, not typed). Both are cosmetic.

The cost of equity uses a total ERP of 6.69% (mature 4.23% plus CRP 2.46%), 69bp above the VAL_BANKS IDR band of 5.0-6.0%, while section 4 says it sits inside the band. The direction is value-conservative, not bullish, but the card requires the deviation to be argued.

flags.message: expected return +80%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is the sum of three sourced items, all named in the report: a dividend yield near nine percent at the current price on a 59% payout, sourced to the annual report's own dividend history [S8]; cost of credit held at the 1.35% nine-month actual and inside the company's unchanged 1.1%-1.4% guidance rather than assumed to collapse [S5]; and the multiple, which is where the previous justification had its arithmetic wrong. At 0.63x book the price capitalises a perpetual ROE of about nine per cent; the warranted multiple at our 11.9% sustainable ROE and 11.9% cost of equity is (0.119-0.04)/(0.1185-0.04) = 1.01x, not the 0.85x quoted before, which was the 10.7% answer mislabelled as 12% [S4][S5]. Section 4 states the implied return and explains why the reverse solver cannot bracket the price on the credit-cost axis: value stays above the price at every charge in its range, so the price is a multiple question, not a provisioning one.
